report:
### Conclusion
Scientific evidence supports the claim that opening a bedroom window or door improves sleep quality by increasing ventilation and preventing carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) buildup.

### Evidence & Mechanism
In sealed bedrooms, human respiration causes $\text{CO}_2$ levels to frequently exceed 1,000–1,500 ppm overnight. Research shows that high $\text{CO}_2$ levels impair sleep quality, causing more frequent awakenings and reduced next-day cognitive performance. Controlled intervention studies demonstrate that opening a window or door increases fresh air exchange, lowers $\text{CO}_2$ concentrations, and measurably improves both subjective sleep satisfaction and objective sleep efficiency.

### Important Caveats
* **Fire Safety vs. Internal Doors:** While opening an internal bedroom door lowers $\text{CO}_2$, fire safety organizations strongly recommend keeping bedroom doors closed at night to slow the spread of smoke, heat, and flames during a home fire.
* **External Disturbances:** Opening windows depends heavily on the outdoor environment. Nighttime traffic noise, pollen, outdoor air pollution, or extreme temperatures can negate the benefits of fresh air and disrupt sleep.

Where outdoor conditions are quiet and clean, opening a window—or using alternative mechanical fresh-air ventilation—provides a reliable, evidence-based boost to sleep quality.

### Sources
* *Indoor Air Journal* (Wiley): https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ina.12435
* *Building and Environment* (ScienceDirect): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605
* Waseda University Research Report: https://www.waseda.jp/top/en/news/86065
* SolutionSphere Safety Review: https://solutionsphere.blog/sleep-with-door-open-or-closed
